newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: INTERVIEW - Leftist wins in UK, France worry ad execs.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Leftist wins in UK, France worry ad execs.

text.p: Marketing executives are worried that recent left-wing election victories in Britain and France will lead to new restrictions on advertising, the head of the world's biggest advertising trade body said on Thursday.

Sonyon Kim, the world president of the International Advertising Association (IAA), told Reuters the arrival on May 1 of a Labour Party government in Britain and the left-wing parliamentary victories in France were cause for concern.
"We are concerned about developments in the UK and France because usually (the arrival of) socialist governments means more regulations," he said in an interview in Amsterdam.

The IAA, a U.S.-based organisation that groups advertising agencies, "advertisers" -- or companies that spend money on advertising -- media companies and other marketing-related firms in 95 countries, promotes advertising self regulation.
Self-regulation is a hot issue for the advertising industry in Europe.
Britain's advertising industry is mostly self-regulated, as are those in the Netherlands, Belgium and Switzerland, while France and Germany have tighter statutory regulations on advertising.

Albert Winninghoff, the president of the European Association of Advertising Agengies, said on Thursday that the advertising industry had been excluded from a general trend within the European Union to liberalise and deregulate various business sectors.

"It's all about breaking down the barriers. Now guess what? Somehow advertising seems to be excluded from the liberalisation and deregulation wave..." he told a two-day European annual conference of the IAA.
"Instead of harmonising liberties -- which lies at the core of the European Union -- advertising is singled out for harmonisation of restrictions," Winninghoff said.
He criticised a system that allowed each of the European Union's 15 member states to have its own rules and restrictions on advertising.

He told the conference that France, for instance, wanted other countries in Europe to adopt its tight restrictions on alchohol and tobacco advertising and that Sweden wanted to "export" throughout Europe its ban on advertising that is targetted to children.
"The European Commission (the European Union's executive body) itself has a couple of nasty initiatives in the works as well," Winninghoff said, without elaborating.
"...we need a wave of advertising deregulation around the world," he said.
Kim, the IAA's world president, told Reuters the IAA decided in a meeting on Wednesday in Amsterdam to hold its "millenium world congress" in London.

The IAA, which holds a world congress every two years, normally chooses the location by rotating around the world region by region. Its 1996 congress, with 2,500 delegates, took place in the South Korean capital of Seoul. The next congress in 1998 will be held in Cairo.
But Kim said the location for the congress in 2000 was chosen in a different manner -- by open bid -- because the year marked the new millenium and so many countries wanted to host it.
Of the dozen countries competing, IAA board members chose a shortlist last night of three locations -- Jerusalem, New York and London.
"Then we selected London," Kim told Reuters.
It was not immediately clear whether the IAA's choice of London as host for its important congress in 2000 was related to the arrival of a Labour government in Britain.
